get on nodes/proxy
get on pods/log
explain: nodes/proxy reaches the kubelet API, including exec. The good-practices page says it bypasses audit logging and admission control, and that even the get verb is enough because websocket requests are authorized as get.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
question: An EncryptionConfiguration lists providers in the order identity, aesgcm. New Secrets are written. Are they encrypted in etcd?
options: Yes, with aesgcm
No: the first provider encrypts new writes, and identity means plain text
Only Secrets created by admins
Yes, with both providers
explain: The guide says if identity is the first provider, at-rest encryption is not enabled. The second provider is only tried when reading data it previously wrote.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
question: A team can do one thing this week on a cluster with no network policies, Baseline pod security, and ingress-nginx admission webhooks. Which change shrinks the most attack paths from a single compromised pod?
options: Enable debug logging
Rename the default service account
Switch base images to distroless
Default-deny network policies with explicit allows, including restricting the webhook to the API server
explain: Under default allow, any pod can reach every service, admin webhook and node port. Default deny turns one foothold into a contained one and directly blocks the IngressNightmare path. Distroless helps too, but only for the images you rebuild.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: Nodes have 3800m allocatable CPU and 14592Mi allocatable memory. Free right now: node-a 1500m and 7592Mi, node-b 800m and 11992Mi, node-c 2000m and 2092Mi. A pod requests 1000m and 6144Mi. Which nodes are feasible?
options: node-a and node-c, because both have enough CPU
All three, because no limits were set
node-b and node-c, because each has the most of one resource
node-a only
explain: Filtering needs every requested resource to fit at the same time. node-b fails on CPU (800 < 1000) and node-c fails on memory (2092 < 6144), so only node-a clears both and scoring has one candidate. Having plenty of one resource does not help when the other is short, which is how a cluster ends up with idle CPU and nowhere to put a pod.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: The user says *any seniority is fine*. Which state change is most faithful to what they said?
options: Leave level as it was (carryover)
Set level to null
Set level to dontcare
Reset the whole state
explain: Null and dontcare both remove the filter, but dontcare also records that the user answered the question. A system that later asks *which level?* would be asking something already answered. Carryover keeps the old filter, which is the wrong behavior here.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
question: Turpin et al. measure unfaithfulness only on examples where the biasing feature points to a wrong answer, using the accuracy drop. Why does that subset make accuracy a usable metric?
options: Because on that subset any answer that follows the bias is wrong, so bias-driven flips show up as lost accuracy
Because models never follow biases toward correct answers, so those examples carry no signal
Because CoT only exists on examples the model gets wrong
Because accuracy on that subset equals the fraction of CoTs that mention the bias
explain: When the bias points to a wrong option, following it costs accuracy, and the authors verified that almost all of the drop is extra bias-consistent answers rather than random noise. The bias does also push toward correct answers on the other subset (accuracy rises there). The metric says nothing directly about mentions; mentions were checked separately (1 of 426).

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
question: A team trains with reward = (tests pass) - penalty x (monitor flag). Flag rate falls from 30% to 2% while test pass rate rises. Which check best distinguishes real improvement from obfuscation?
options: Check that the CoTs still read fluently and stay on topic
Measure hacking with a signal independent of the CoT, such as reverting test edits or a held-out action check
Ask the trained model whether it is hacking
Re-run the same CoT monitor with a higher temperature
explain: Obfuscated CoTs are fluent and on topic by construction, and the trained policy is optimized against this monitor, so rerunning it adds little. Asking the model trusts the very channel in question. Only a behavior measure that does not route through the CoT (like Baker's revert-the-test-edits check) can reveal hacks the monitor no longer sees.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
question: Someone optimizes the kernel from 24 ms to 12 ms. What is the new batch time and the new SM utilization?
options: 49 ms, utilization 24.5 percent
30.5 ms, utilization unchanged at 39.3 percent
49 ms, utilization 39.3 percent
37 ms, utilization 32.4 percent
explain: 20 + 16 + 12 + 1 = 49 ms, and the SMs are now busy 12 of those 49 ms, which is 24.5 percent. Halving the kernel bought 19.7 percent of wall time and made the imbalance worse. The 37 ms of host and copy time is where the remaining win lives.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: You chunk the host decode too, and measure the host stage at 8.00 ms per chunk (kernel stays 6.00 ms). What paces the pipeline and what is the 4-chunk time?
options: The host, at 8.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms
The kernel, at 6.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 6.00 = 36.25 ms
Neither; the host runs on a different device so it does not enter the makespan
The H2D copy, since it is the stage directly after the host
explain: The host is just another single-server stage in the pipeline, and the makespan is set by whichever stage is largest. At 8.00 ms it overtakes the 6.00 ms kernel, giving (8.00 + 4.00 + 6.00 + 0.25) + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms, with 2.00 ms of SM idle per chunk. The fix is more host parallelism (more decode threads or loader workers), not more CUDA streams.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: Why does Margin-MSE train on the score difference instead of asking the student to reproduce the teacher's raw score?
options: Because the teacher's raw scores are not available after training
Because MSE cannot be computed on raw scores
Because the margin is always positive
Because different architectures produce scores on very different ranges, and ranking only depends on order and gaps
explain: The paper observed that cross-encoders, dot-product models and others have distinct score ranges. Matching margins lets the student keep its natural range while learning the teacher's preferences. The margin can even be negative when the teacher disagrees with the label.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Two ciphertexts were made with the same one-time pad. What can Eve compute without knowing the key?
options: Nothing: each ciphertext is perfectly secret
The key itself, directly
Only the lengths of the messages
The XOR of the two plaintexts
explain: XORing the ciphertexts cancels the key and leaves m1 XOR m2. From there, guessing likely words in one message reveals the other. The key itself only falls out once Eve also knows a plaintext.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Which property must a hash have so that nobody can create two different contracts with the same digest, one innocent and one malicious?
options: Preimage resistance
Second-preimage resistance
Avalanche effect
Collision resistance
explain: The attacker controls both documents, so they only need any pair that collides: that is collision resistance, the property MD5 and SHA-1 lost (next lesson).

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Why did Debian's broken generator still produce different keys on different runs, hiding the bug for almost two years?
options: The kernel added entropy later anyway
OpenSSL used the time of day
SSH re-randomised the keys
The process ID was still mixed in, giving about 32,767 variants
explain: Russ Cox notes the PID kept the output from being completely deterministic. If every key had been identical, the bug would likely have been caught quickly.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: In TLS 1.3, which message stops a man in the middle from substituting their own Diffie-Hellman key share?
options: ClientHello
The AEAD tag on application data
The server's random value
CertificateVerify, the server's signature over the handshake
explain: The key shares are just DH values. CertificateVerify signs the transcript, including them, with the key the CA vouched for, so substituted shares fail verification.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
question: ROBOT's authors could make facebook.com's key sign a message. Why did they say the certificate did not need to be revoked?
options: Because Facebook's certificate had already expired
Because the attack used the server as an oracle to perform operations, without extracting the private key
Because signatures made with a Bleichenbacher oracle are invalid
Because RSA keys cannot be revoked
explain: A Bleichenbacher oracle makes the server's key decrypt or sign attacker-chosen values one step at a time, but the key never leaves the server. Fixing the server (or removing RSA key exchange) closes the oracle; the key stays secret.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
question: A team replaces `==` with this check: `return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b)) == 0`. It visits every byte. Is it a good fix for comparing HMAC tags?
options: Yes, it is exactly as good as hmac.compare_digest
No: summing is slower than ==
No: zip silently stops at the shorter input, and hand-written loops are not guaranteed constant time; use hmac.compare_digest
Yes, as long as tags are hex strings
explain: zip stops at the shorter argument, so a short or empty tag can compare equal to a prefix (an empty tag passes). Interpreter and compiler details can also reintroduce timing differences. The standard library function is designed for this job.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
question: A team signs both webhook payloads and password-reset links with one Ed25519 key and no labels. What is the risk?
options: A signature produced for one message type may be accepted where the other is expected, if an attacker can get suitable bytes signed
Ed25519 cannot sign URLs
The key will wear out twice as fast
None, signatures are always bound to their purpose
explain: Signatures bind to bytes, not to meaning. Separate keys, or a purpose label inside the signed data, ensure a webhook signature can never be presented as a reset link signature.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: You compose a data tensor A with B and get R = A o B. Which property does the CuTe documentation guarantee?
options: R has the same shape as A
R is always injective
R(i) = A(B(i)) for all i in B's domain, and R accepts B's coordinates
R has the same strides as B
explain: Composition's post-conditions are compatible(B, R) and R(i) == A(B(i)). B defines the domain, so R takes B's coordinates; A defines where those land.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: Why can't a CPU vendor simply add many more DDR5 channels to every socket?
options: DDR5 does not support more than two channels per socket
More channels would make memory non-coherent
Each DDR5 channel is a wide parallel interface that needs many pins (Sun et al. cite 288 per channel), and the package pin budget is fixed
Linux cannot address more than eight memory channels
explain: DDR is a wide parallel interface. Capacity and bandwidth scale with the number of channels, and each channel eats a lot of pins. A serial CXL link delivers more bandwidth per pin, which is why it is attractive for expansion.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: TPP does not promote a slow-tier page on its first NUMA hinting fault if the page is on the inactive LRU list. What problem does this avoid?
options: Deadlock between the fault handler and reclaim
Ping-pong: an infrequently used page is promoted, then quickly demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth
Running out of tier-16 memory
Breaking cache coherence on the CXL link
explain: A single touch does not prove a page is hot. Promoting it would push something else out of DRAM, and under pressure the promoted page would soon be demoted again. Requiring the page to be on the active LRU adds hysteresis: a page must show repeated use before it moves, so it stops flipping back and forth.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: Which statement about Base64 is correct?
options: It is a weak form of encryption that needs a short key
It is an encoding that anyone can reverse without a key, so it protects nothing
It is a hash, so the original cannot be recovered
It is only used for images
explain: Base64 (RFC 4648) maps bytes to 64 printable characters so they survive text channels. Decoding needs no secret. When officials said the reporter had 'unencrypted the source code' or 'decoded the HTML source code', they made an ordinary step sound like an attack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: Which change did the 2021 rulemaking make to the security research exemption, according to GitHub's summary?
options: It made circumvention tools legal to sell
It removed the condition that the research must not violate any other law
It ended the exemption
It extended the exemption to servers you do not own without permission
explain: GitHub explains that before 2021 a violation of another law such as the CFAA could also cost you the DMCA exemption. The Office recommended removing that condition, while noting researchers must still consider other laws themselves.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Under the ISC2 complaint procedure, who may complain that a member breached Canon III (diligent and competent service to principals)?
options: Any member of the public
Only principals, meaning those with an employer or contractor relationship with the member
Only other certified professionals
Nobody: Canon III is advisory
explain: ISC2's procedure says anyone may complain about Canons I or II, only principals about Canon III, and only other professionals who subscribe to a code of ethics about Canon IV.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: Why is tuning the mixture directly on downstream benchmarks risky, beyond its cost?
options: Benchmarks are measured in accuracy, not loss
Downstream tuning always picks uniform weights
The mixture can overfit to the specific benchmarks used, which may not reflect the many tasks the model will face
explain: A pretrained model is used for many tasks nobody listed in advance. A mixture tuned to a handful of benchmarks can trade away performance elsewhere. DoReMi deliberately uses no downstream data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: You start DoReMi from uniform reference weights on a corpus where one domain is tiny. After one round, results are no better than baseline. What is the paper's recommended next move?
options: Run iterated DoReMi: train a new reference model on the round-1 weights and run again
Increase the proxy to 1B parameters
Set the smoothing c to 0 so weak domains disappear
Copy the published Pile weights
explain: On GLaM, round 1 from uniform weights was only comparable to the baseline, and round 2 matched downstream-tuned weights. A suboptimal reference gives a suboptimal excess loss; iterating fixes the reference. Bigger proxies did worse in the paper.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Why do pipelines run heuristic rules before a perplexity filter or a model-based classifier?
options: Rules are more accurate than models
The order does not matter for cost
Rules only count words and symbols, so they cheaply remove obvious junk before the expensive model-based steps run
Perplexity filters only work on text that has been deduplicated
explain: A rule is a few counts per page; a language model or classifier must process every token. Removing describable junk first shrinks what the costly steps must score. Orders still vary between pipelines.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
explain: Block 2 (17 divided by 8 is 2, rounded down), lane 1 (the remainder). Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: A Purview-style rule finds a Luhn-valid 16-digit number with no keywords or dates within 300 characters. What should the confidence be?
options: Low: pattern and checksum without supporting context
High: the checksum proves it is a card
None: without a keyword it is discarded
High, because test numbers are excluded
explain: In Microsoft's documented definition, pattern plus checksum alone is the low-confidence pattern (65). High confidence (85) needs one of the context conditions. About 1 in 10 random numbers pass Luhn, so the checksum alone proves little.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: A team wants to encrypt an `is_vip` boolean column but still filter on it. Why is deterministic encryption a poor choice?
options: Deterministic encryption cannot encrypt booleans
It is slower than randomized encryption
It requires a secure enclave
With only two values, each ciphertext appears in many rows, and counting them (plus any known fact about one row) reveals every row's value
explain: Deterministic encryption maps each plaintext to one ciphertext. With two possible values, there are two ciphertexts; knowing the VIP rate or one VIP customer decodes all rows. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this for True/False columns.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: A DLP rule has 95% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Real leaks are 1 in 1,000 messages. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 9%
About 95%
About 50%
About 1%
explain: Per 200,000 messages: 190 true alerts and about 1,998 false ones, so 190 / 2,188 is about 8.7%. Recall is 95%, but precision is low because clean messages vastly outnumber leaks.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: Branch servers had disk encryption switched on years after deployment, and the product encrypted only newly written data. Why does a later cryptographic erase not sanitise them?
options: The data written before encryption was enabled is still plaintext on the disks, and destroying the key does nothing to it
Crypto erase never works on servers
The keys were too short
Crypto erase needs internet access
explain: Cryptographic erase only removes access to what was encrypted. SP 800-88 Rev. 2 makes 'no sensitive data previously stored in plaintext' a precondition, and the SEC order describes exactly this flaw.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature, and the sampler draws from one shared RNG stream. What does request B's token depend on?
options: How many draws the sampler already consumed for other requests, so B's token depends on the traffic around it.
Nothing beyond its own seed, since the seed fully determines the stream.
Only the temperature, because the seed is consumed once at startup.
The order in which atomic adds landed in the final GEMM.
explain: A shared stream makes the position in the stream part of the request's input, and that position is set by the queue. Seeding the stream fixes the sequence of numbers, not which element of it your request receives. Per-request generator state is what removes the dependency.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: Why does the toy simulator put a sequence number between the time and the event in each queue entry?
options: So events at the same simulated time pop in a fixed order on every run
To make the heap faster
To count how many messages were lost
So that later events can be cancelled
explain: Two events can share a timestamp. Without a deterministic tie-breaker their order would depend on incidental details (here, Python would even try to compare the event payloads). The sequence number makes the order a function of the order of scheduling, which is itself determined by the seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
question: Which item is policy as code?
options: A Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs unit tests
A Rego file stating that no security group may allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0
A wiki page listing the company's security standards
explain: Policy as code is a rule a machine evaluates. The Terraform file is infrastructure as code, the workflow is pipeline code, and a wiki page is policy that nobody's pipeline can enforce.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
question: After a CI vendor breach, which kind of pipeline credential needs no rotation at all?
options: A long-lived cloud access key stored as a project secret
An SSH deploy key stored in the CI service
A registry token kept in a context
A cloud role assumed through OIDC, where the CI service stores only the role name
explain: With OIDC the CI service holds no long-lived secret: it presents a short-lived signed token each run. Stolen role names grant nothing. Every stored key or token must be rotated.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret
question: Grzelak's attack adds a resource that names an attacker's provider to the state. Why does a required manual approval before apply not stop it?
options: Approvals are optional in Terraform
terraform init downloads the provider and Terraform runs its code while planning, before anyone is asked to approve
The provider runs only after apply
State files are not read during plan
explain: Grzelak notes that even if the reviewer rejects the plan, the code has already executed. That is why the post recommends pre-installed providers in an immutable image and a read-only role for the plan step.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
question: During an outage an engineer raised a database's connection limit in the console, and the fix should stay. What is the right drift response?
options: Run apply to revert it, since code is the source of truth
Codify it: change the Terraform code through a pull request to match, using refresh-only planning to reconcile state, so the next apply does not undo it
Delete the database from state
Ignore the drift alerts from now on
explain: This is the codify path. Reverting would reintroduce the outage; ignoring trains everyone to ignore drift alerts.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
question: Spot the bug: a colleague's loss is `(ce * masked).sum() / masked.sum()`, the plain average over masked tokens, with t still drawn uniformly. What changes?
options: Nothing; it is the same quantity
The loss now includes visible tokens

Summed over the batch and divided by the total masked count, every masked token gets equal weight, so heavily masked sequences dominate; the 1/t factor is lost and it is no longer the likelihood bound
The model will learn to predict [MASK] tokens
explain: Over a large batch the ratio tends to E[sum of masked losses] / E[count]: the unweighted MaskGIT-style objective with no 1/t, which LLaDA notes lacks a link to maximum likelihood. The principled loss divides each sequence by t L. Dividing each sequence by its own masked count would actually be fine: with uniform t the count is uniform on 0 to L, which is the exact-count form LLaDA uses for likelihoods (skip sequences with nothing masked).

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Where diffusion LMs stand: results, block diffusion, and limits
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct beats GPT-4o on reversal poem completion but loses badly on forward completion. What is the best reading?
options: Training to predict tokens from both sides removes the directional bias, while GPT-4o's much larger training gives it a big edge in the direction it was trained on
LLaDA is a stronger model overall
The benchmark is broken because the scores do not add to 100
GPT-4o was evaluated with a causal mask removed
explain: LLaDA's forward and reversal scores are close (51.8 vs 45.6) because its objective covers all conditioning directions. GPT-4o is far stronger in the forward direction (82.7) but falls to 34.3 in reverse, the reversal curse. Neither result says LLaDA is better overall.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
question: Using the formula, how long does an ideal transfer of a 4096-token Qwen3-32B prompt (256 KiB per token) take over a 400 Gb/s link?
options: About 2.7 ms
About 21.5 ms
About 344 ms
About 172 ms
explain: 4096 x 262,144 B = 1,073,741,824 B (1 GiB). 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s, so 1.074 GB / 50 GB/s = 21.5 ms. Half of the 43 ms needed for 8192 tokens, because KV size grows linearly with prompt length.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: After deletion, which piece of the PHOTO.JPG directory entry is gone for good?
options: The first character of its name
Its size
Its first cluster number
Its extension
explain: Deletion overwrote only the name's first byte with 0xE5. Size, first cluster and extension remain, which is why tools show deleted names as ?HOTO.JPG or _HOTO.JPG.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: With the default data=ordered journal mode, what can the ext4 journal give you after a file is deleted?
options: Possibly an older copy of the metadata block holding the file's inode, with its extents
A full copy of the file's content
Nothing, because the journal is erased on deletion
The user name of whoever deleted it
explain: data=ordered sends metadata, not file data, through the journal. Older inode blocks in the journal can point recovery tools to the content blocks. ext4 does not log who deleted a file.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: The USB stick is lost. What can still show that the user browsed its folder `E:\Q3`?
options: Only the stick itself
The master file table of the laptop's C: drive
SRUM
ShellBags in the user's hives, and LNK and Jump List entries pointing to `E:\Q3`
explain: ShellBags record navigated folders, and LNK and Jump List entries record opened files with their paths and volume serial, all stored on the laptop. The laptop's C: MFT does not index files on E:.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Why does wiping a file often fail to hide that something was wiped?
options: Wiping tools are blocked by NTFS
The wipe overwrites the content but leaves traces such as the tool's execution artefacts and change journal records of the overwrite
Wiped data can always be recovered by carving
Windows keeps a copy of every wiped file in SRUM
explain: SP 800-86 notes wiping is effective at preventing collection of the content itself, so carving does not undo it. But running a tool and rewriting a file leave execution and journal traces. SRUM stores usage statistics, not files.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: In the toy example, what happens to the optimal policy as $\beta$ grows very large?
options: It approaches the reference distribution: 50%, 30%, 20%
It puts all mass on B, the highest reward
It becomes uniform over A, B and C
It puts all mass on A, the reference's favorite
explain: Reweighting by $\exp(r/\beta)$ approaches multiplying everything by 1 as $\beta$ grows, so the optimum returns to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. At $\beta = 10$ it is already 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%. Small $\beta$ is what collapses it onto B.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Your feedback log has 2,000 thumbs-up and 20,000 thumbs-down responses. Following the KTO paper's guidance with $\lambda_U = 1$, which $\lambda_D$ is in range?
options: 0.1, to down-weight the rare class
1, the default
explain: The ratio $\lambda_D n_D / (\lambda_U n_U)$ should land in [1, 1.5]. With $n_D/n_U = 0.1$, $\lambda_D$ must be between 10 and 15, so 12 fits. Leaving it at 1 lets the undesirable class dominate the gradient.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Dual writes have been on for a week, but the backfill has not run. A read from the new Subscriptions table for a customer who subscribed two years ago and has not changed since returns nothing. What happened?
options: The dual write to the new table failed for this customer
Nothing went wrong: untouched old objects only reach the new store through the backfill
The new table needs a read replica before it can serve reads
Dual writes copy old rows lazily on the first read, so the next read will succeed
explain: Dual writes only cover writes made after they were turned on. Stripe also copied objects lazily whenever they were *updated*, but an object nobody touches is copied only by the backfill. This is why reads must not move until the backfill and a completeness check are done.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: Midway through phase 3, the new write path for prorations is found to compute the wrong amount. Most other paths already write the new store first and archive to the old one. What is the safest response?
options: Restore the new store from last night's backup
Pause all writes until the bug is fixed
Delete the old store so the two cannot disagree
Flip the prorations path back to the old write order; the old store is still current because every path still writes it
explain: In phase 3 every write still reaches the old store (as the primary or as an archive), so it is complete. Rolling one path back by a flag is cheap. That safety disappears in phase 4, which is why it comes last.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: A read takes exactly 1,024 ns. In which hist() bucket does it appear?
explain: 1024 = 2^10, so b = 10 and the bucket is [2^10, 2^11) = [1K, 2K). Bucket intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound; only 0 and 1 get single-value buckets.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: An activation tensor after ReLU has range [0, 6]. Using asymmetric int8 with q_min = -128, what are S and Z?
explain: S = (6 - 0) / (127 - (-128)) = 6/255 = 0.0235, and Z = round(-128 - 0/S) = -128. Real 0 maps to the lowest code, so all 256 levels cover [0, 6]. The symmetric choice (S = 6/127, Z = 0) would waste the 128 negative codes on values ReLU never produces.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: A wake-word model meets its accuracy target in float but loses 6 points after full-integer PTQ with per-channel weights. Calibration data is representative. What should you try next?
options: Quantization-aware training, or 16-bit activations if the runtime supports them
Per-tensor weights instead of per-channel
Remove calibration and use dynamic range quantization on a microcontroller with no float unit
Prune the model to 90% sparsity
explain: Per-channel weights and good calibration are already in place, so the remaining error likely comes from activations or from a small model's sensitivity. QAT lets the model adapt to rounding, and 16x8 mode reduces activation error. Per-tensor would be worse, and dynamic range keeps float outputs that an integer-only MCU cannot run.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
question: You installed the NetScaler fix on 11 October 2023, the day after it shipped. Why could an attacker still be using your gateway on 20 October?
options: The fix did not install
A session cookie stolen before the fix stayed valid until sessions were killed
The fix turned off MFA
NetScaler cannot be patched
explain: Exploitation began in late August. The fix stops new leaks but does not invalidate tokens already taken; NetScaler's guidance was to kill all active and persistent sessions after updating.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
question: M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean time to exploit of -7 days. What does the negative sign mean for an edge patch process?
options: Patches arrive a week before bugs are found
On average, exploitation begins before a fix exists, so fast patching must be paired with checking for compromise that happened earlier
Attackers stopped using n-days
Vendors publish advisories a week late on purpose
explain: Negative TTE means exploitation precedes the patch. Speed still matters (it stops mass exploitation after disclosure), but forensic triage is what deals with the earlier window.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
question: Barracuda asked customers to replace ESG appliances 'regardless of patch version level'. What does that tell a defender about patching?
options: Patches from Barracuda were never released
Once an appliance may hold persistence the vendor cannot reliably remove, patching cannot restore trust; only new hardware can
Email gateways cannot be patched
Replacement is always cheaper than patching
explain: The patch fixed the bug, but the vendor could not be confident that software updates removed the intruder from compromised devices. The same logic drives rebuilds for Ivanti and hard resets for Cisco.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: A team trains with a hard rule 'reward = -1 if truncated at 8K tokens' and sees training become unstable as responses approach 8K. Which change follows the DAPO findings?
options: Raise the penalty to -10 so the model learns faster
Remove the correctness reward for long responses
Mask truncated samples from the loss, or ramp the penalty linearly over a soft zone before the limit
Lower the learning rate only for long responses
explain: Overlong filtering (masking) and soft overlong punishment both reduce reward noise from punishing reasoning that was merely cut off. A bigger cliff adds more noise, not less.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Ana's laptop runs signature antivirus only. Word starts PowerShell, which downloads nothing to disk and connects to a remote server. Why might the antivirus stay silent?
options: It judges files one at a time, and no file here matches a known-bad signature; the suspicious part is the sequence of behaviours
Antivirus cannot run on laptops that have Office installed
PowerShell disables antivirus whenever it starts
Antivirus only scans email, never processes
explain: Signature antivirus answers a per-file question. Each file here (winword.exe, powershell.exe) is legitimate. The signal is in the relationships: an Office app starting a shell that then goes online. Recording and correlating those relationships is what EDR adds.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: An admin writes `<ProcessAccess onmatch="include" />` with no rules inside, expecting to see every process access. What does Sysmon log for event 10?
options: Every process access
Only access to lsass.exe
Nothing
Only accesses by unsigned programs
explain: An include filter logs only events that match a rule; with no rules nothing matches, so nothing is logged. To log everything you would use an empty exclude filter (which is usually far too noisy for event 10).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: A path rule allows `C:\Windows\*`. Why is that weaker than a publisher rule for Microsoft-signed binaries?
options: Path rules are slower to evaluate
Publisher rules also block Microsoft Office
Some folders under `C:\Windows` are writable by ordinary users, so anything a user copies there is allowed; a publisher rule requires the file's signature instead
Path rules only work for DLLs
explain: A path rule trusts a location. Microsoft's default-rules page names `C:\Windows\Temp` as user-writable, so a path rule over the Windows folder lets users run their own files from there. A publisher rule trusts a signature the user cannot forge.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: Which of these would an endpoint sensor on employees' laptops record?
options: A forwarding rule created in cloud webmail from the attacker's own browser
A login to the company VPN appliance
powershell.exe on a laptop opening a handle to lsass.exe
The content of a TLS connection to a web server
explain: Process-to-process handle requests on a monitored host are exactly what sensors record. The webmail rule and VPN login happen on systems with no sensor, and TLS content is encrypted; only metadata such as the destination is visible.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
question: Your entity graph has a cluster of 40,000 company records that should be about 30 companies. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blocking was too strict
A few false links between large clusters, chained by transitive connected components
The prior lambda was set too low
explain: Strict blocking and a low prior both cause missed links, which make clusters too small. Giant clusters come from false edges: connected components chains them, so one bad edge between two big clusters merges both.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: A tenant blocks device code flow everywhere except for the SharePoint resource. A user's session began with a device code sign-in to SharePoint. They then try to open Exchange Online in the same session. What does Microsoft document?
options: Exchange is blocked, because the session is protocol tracked and the device code policy applies to later requests from it
Exchange is allowed because the user signed in normally
Exchange prompts for a new device code
The policy is ignored for refresh tokens
explain: Microsoft's example is exactly this: protocol tracking keeps the session marked as device code through later refreshes, so a sign-in to Exchange in that session is blocked by the authentication flows policy.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: Why does Microsoft recommend rolling the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key at least every 30 days?
options: Because anyone holding a copy of that key can create tickets Entra ID trusts for synced users, so a regular rollover limits how long a stolen copy stays useful
Because Kerberos tickets expire after 30 days
To change the encryption from AES to RC4
Because the key is needed to sync passwords
explain: Entra ID decrypts Seamless SSO tickets with that key, so a stolen copy works like a silver ticket key for the cloud sign-in. Rolling it regularly, and after any AD compromise, retires old copies.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why attackers then reuse existing code
question: Why did NX alone not end memory-corruption exploits?
options: Because NX can be turned off by any program
Because NX only applies to 32-bit processes
Because NX leaks the canary
Because attackers could still redirect control to code that is already executable, such as functions and instruction sequences in libc
explain: NX blocks running data as code, but a hijacked return or function pointer can target existing executable code. That is the core insight of return-into-libc and of Shacham's return-oriented programming paper.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Protecting returns: shadow stacks and pointer authentication
question: An overflow writes past a buffer using an index, skipping the canary and changing only the saved return address. Which mitigation still catches it at return?
options: A hardware shadow stack, because it compares the return address itself with a protected copy
The stack canary
FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO
explain: The canary is untouched, so its check passes. The shadow stack compares the actual return address with a copy that normal stores cannot change, so any modification is caught.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Turning mitigations on and checking a binary
question: `readelf -lW prog` shows a GNU_RELRO segment, and `readelf -d prog` shows `FLAGS_1 PIE` but no BIND_NOW or NOW flag. What should you conclude?
options: Partial RELRO and PIE: .got.plt is still writable; add -Wl,-z,now
Full RELRO and PIE
No RELRO, because BIND_NOW is missing
Not PIE, because BIND_NOW is missing
explain: GNU_RELRO alone is partial RELRO. Full RELRO also needs immediate binding (BIND_NOW / NOW). PIE is indicated separately by the PIE flag and the DYN file type.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
question: An MoE is trained on 64 GPUs, each micro-batch holding 2 sequences, with the balance loss computed per micro-batch. Analysis shows every expert is used about equally on code, math and prose. Which change most directly allows domain specialization?
options: Raise alpha so the balance loss is stronger
Add a router z-loss
Synchronize the expert counts $f_i$ across all micro-batches and compute the balance loss on the global batch
Raise the capacity factor
explain: With 2 sequences per micro-batch, the loss forces each sequence to spread evenly, so code tokens cannot concentrate on code experts. Counting $f_i$ over the global batch only requires the corpus mix to be balanced. A larger alpha tightens the same wrong constraint; the z-loss is about logit size; capacity only changes dropping.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
question: On H100 at $d = 128$, exponentials take about 50% of the matmul time. If FP8 matmuls run at 2x the FP16 rate and MUFU is unchanged, what does that ratio become?
options: 25%, because FP8 values are half the size
50%, unchanged
About 100%
About 200%
explain: $T_{exp}/T_{MMA} = r_{MMA}/(4 d\, r_{exp})$. Doubling $r_{MMA}$ doubles the ratio from 0.5 to 1.0: the exponentials now take as long as the matmuls. The FlashAttention-3 paper says exactly this: "the matmul throughput doubles but the exponential throughput stays the same."

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
question: What is the main reason FlashAttention-4 uses the 2-CTA MMA mode in the backward pass?
options: To double the tensor core FLOPs available to each CTA
To cut shared memory traffic (each CTA stages half of operand B) and halve dQ atomic adds
To make the backward pass deterministic
To fit five accumulators in tensor memory
explain: The backward pass is limited by shared memory bandwidth (3328 vs 2560 cycles). Pairing CTAs means each stages half of B, and the dS exchange lets each CTA own half of the dQ tile, halving atomics. Peak FLOPs are unchanged, and determinism comes from the separate semaphore mode.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
question: Doubling Euler steps from 8 to 16 on the toy cut the endpoint error from about 0.135 to about 0.067. What does that ratio indicate?
options: Error is roughly proportional to step size, so Euler is first order
Euler is a second-order method
The flow is straight
The network is overfitting
explain: Halving h roughly halved the error, which is first-order behavior: global error proportional to h. A second-order method like Heun would cut it by about 4x.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
question: You fix the race by making the increment one atomic step (and remove tmp from the spec): `Inc(p) == pc[p] = "inc" /\ x' = x + 1 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "done"]`. What does TLC report for N = 2?
options: Still a violation, because two processes can run Inc in the same step
No error: every step increments x by 1, so x = 2 once both are done
A deadlock error, because Inc can never be enabled
It cannot check it, since x' = x + 1 is an assignment
explain: Next allows exactly one process to take one step at a time, so nothing interleaves inside Inc. TLC confirms it: 4 distinct states, no error (8 states for N = 3). In PlusCal the fix is to put the read and write under one label.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
question: In TwoPhase, the TM receives a Prepared message, which changes only tmPrepared. What does TCommit see under the refinement mapping?
options: A Prepare step by that RM
A stuttering step, because rmState is unchanged
A violation, since TCommit has no TM
Nothing: refinement checking skips steps that change hidden variables
explain: The mapping exposes only rmState. A step that leaves rmState unchanged maps to a stuttering step, which every TLA+ spec allows. TLC does not skip it; it checks that it is a stutter.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: A small Rust function parses a length-prefixed packet using unsafe pointer arithmetic, with inputs up to 64 bytes. You want a counterexample if any input can cause out-of-bounds access, with minimal annotation. Which fits best?
options: TLA+ with TLC
P
TLAPS
Kani with a harness over any 64-byte input
explain: This is a code-level, bounded question about one function: exactly what Kani's harnesses and kani::any() are for, and Kani checks for undefined behavior in unsafe code. TLA+, P and TLAPS work on design models, not on the Rust code.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: A team turns on FP8 GEMMs for every linear layer and expects peak memory to halve. It barely changes. Why?
options: FP8 tensors are padded to 16 bits in memory
Most memory is master weights, gradients, optimizer moments and activations that FP8 GEMM inputs do not touch
The amax history uses more memory than the weights
Tensor cores cannot read FP8 from memory
explain: FP8 GEMMs change compute, not the 12 to 16 bytes per parameter of training state. FP8-LM cut memory by moving the gradient and first moment to FP8 and the master weight and second moment to FP16, and DeepSeek-V3 caches activations in FP8.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: Why does the recipe use 16x16 2D blocks for weights but 1x16 blocks for activations and gradients?
options: 2D blocks are faster for every tensor
Activations cannot be transposed
1x16 blocks are required by E4M3
Weights are reused in both Fprop and Dgrad (transposed), so a scale shared over a square block keeps the two quantized copies identical; activations and gradients benefit more from finer 1x16 scaling
explain: The chain-rule mismatch matters most for weights, and weights can adapt to coarser scaling during training. The report found training less sensitive to inconsistency in activations, so they keep the more accurate 1x16 blocks.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
question: Your app's 'find friends by email' endpoint returns full profiles for matches and has a 10,000 per hour limit per IP address. What is the most important change?
options: Raise the per-IP limit so real users are not blocked
Hash the email addresses before uploading
Switch the response to XML
Cap lookups per account, return only a suggestion, and honour a discoverability setting
explain: Per-IP limits fall to proxies, and hashing emails does not stop matching (the server still answers per identifier). The structural fixes limit volume per identity, minimise what a match reveals, and let users opt out of being found.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
question: At USD 1 per thousand solves, how much does a CAPTCHA on every attempt add to a 100,000-attempt campaign?
options: USD 1
USD 100
USD 10
explain: 100,000 / 1,000 x USD 1 = USD 100. Compare that with the campaign's revenue (lesson 2): a challenge alone often only trims profit.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
question: A developer proposes 'block any card number that fails the Luhn check, and treat Luhn-valid numbers as low risk'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, Luhn proves the card exists
Luhn only detects typos; a valid check digit says nothing about whether the card is real, funded or the user's own
Luhn is only for debit cards
Luhn checks are illegal under PCI DSS
explain: The check digit is public arithmetic designed to catch typing errors. Rejecting failures early is fine for usability, but passing it carries no risk information.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
question: At a threshold your control has precision 0.18 and recall 0.89 on a base rate of 0.5%. What does precision 0.18 mean for customers?
options: 18% of fraud is caught
Of the orders you blocked, 82% were from good customers
18% of good customers are blocked
The model is wrong 18% of the time
explain: Precision is TP / (TP + FP). At 0.18, only 18% of blocked orders were fraud; the other 82% were honest customers. With rare fraud, even a small false positive rate creates this.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
question: A month after your 4-cards-per-device rule launched, its hits fell 90%, but fraud losses are unchanged and many devices now try exactly 3 cards. What does this indicate?
options: The rule solved the problem
Card networks changed their rules
A data pipeline bug
Attackers adapted to the threshold; losses, not rule hits, measure success
explain: Clustering just under a threshold with flat losses is classic adaptation. Combine the count with outcomes and amounts, avoid revealing exact thresholds, and track loss as the ground truth.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
question: A checkpointer's fsync of a data file returns EIO. Which response is safe on Linux?
options: Call fsync again until it returns 0, then continue
Crash deliberately and replay the WAL from the last checkpoint
Close the file, reopen it and fsync the new descriptor
Ignore it: the next checkpoint will write the page again
explain: The failed pages may already be marked clean and dropped, so a retry can report success with the data lost, and a fresh descriptor may not see the old error at all. The WAL still holds every change since the last checkpoint, so redo can rebuild the pages.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
question: In the run log, what does the line '#1045 NEW cov: 6 ... DE: "TLV1"' tell you?
options: The fuzzer crashed at execution 1045
The user supplied a dictionary file containing TLV1
Input number 1045 reached new coverage, built with a dictionary entry TLV1 that comparison tracing discovered
The corpus was minimised to 6 inputs
explain: NEW means new coverage and a new corpus entry; the DE field names the dictionary entry used. No dictionary file was supplied: trace-cmp observed the comparison against TLV1 and learned the token.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Crash triage: deduplicate, minimise, root-cause, fix
question: Two crash files both end in memcpy inside parse_tlv, but one is reached from load_config() and one from load_profile(). How should a stack-hash deduplicator with the top 3 frames treat them?
options: Always as one bug, because the faulting line is the same
As zero bugs, because memcpy is a library function
As two separate buckets, since frame 3 (the caller of parse_tlv) differs, even though they may be one root cause
It cannot hash them without source code
explain: Stack hashes include callers, so different paths into the same bug make different buckets. That is the over-counting Klees et al. measured. A human or a fix-based check (does one patch fix both?) merges them.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
question: Why does AFLNet use the server's response codes as feedback, in addition to code coverage?
options: Response codes are faster to compute than coverage
They replace the need for seeds
They reveal which protocol state the server reached, so sequences reaching new states are kept even when coverage alone is ambiguous
They detect memory corruption
explain: Its README describes identifying server states from response codes and steering towards progressive regions of the state space. State feedback complements coverage: the same code can run in different states.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
question: Under Project Zero's Full 90 policy, a vendor ships a patch on day 47. When are the technical details published?
options: Day 47, with the patch
Day 77, 30 days after the patch
Day 90
Never, once a patch exists
explain: Full X means details are published on day X regardless of when the patch shipped, unless the vendor asks for earlier release. Day 47 to day 90 is the window for users to update.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
question: Using the Jaro-Winkler formula with p = 0.1: `dwayne` vs `duane` has Jaro similarity 0.8222 and shares only the first letter. What is the Jaro-Winkler score?
options: 0.8222, because a prefix of 1 earns no boost
explain: JW = J + l x p x (1 - J) = 0.8222 + 1 x 0.1 x 0.1778 = 0.8400. Every shared leading character (up to 4) moves the score a tenth of the remaining distance toward 1.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
question: Why does the table store each model under *all* ordered basis pairs rather than just one canonical pair?
options: To make the table smaller
Because the canonical pair might be hidden or missing in the scene, and any visible pair must still be able to find the model
Because a single pair does not define a frame under similarity transforms
To avoid quantization errors at bin edges
explain: Occlusion and clutter are the whole point. If only basis (p1, p2) were stored and p1 were hidden, the model could never be found. Storing all n(n-1) bases means any two visible model points can serve as the scene basis.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: You have hundreds of frames of the same field from one night and want to stack them. Which approach fits best?
options: Blind-solve each frame against an all-sky quad index, every time
Use SIFT descriptors on the star patches
Register frames to each other with triangle asterism matching (as in astroalign), solving just one frame blind if you need sky coordinates
Assume the frames are already aligned
explain: Frame-to-frame registration has a tiny search space, where triangle matching plus RANSAC is fast and reliable. Blind all-sky solving is for when you do not know where the image points; doing it per frame is wasteful.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
question: A teammate's 'nearby drivers' query returns all drivers whose geohash starts with the rider's 6-character geohash, then sorts by haversine distance. Riders near cell edges complain that close drivers never appear. What is the bug?
options: Haversine is inaccurate under 1 km and should be replaced by Euclidean distance
Geohash should be computed latitude first, not longitude first
Only the center cell is searched, so drivers in the 8 neighboring cells are never candidates
The prefix should be longer so cells are smaller
explain: Candidate generation must cover the whole circle. A rider near an edge has close drivers in neighboring cells, which share a shorter prefix or none at all. A longer prefix makes it worse; the fix is the center cell plus its 8 neighbors at a precision matched to the radius.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
question: Dropping the minus one half from the source coordinate produces a shift of (s - 1) / 2 source pixels. When is that shift exactly zero?
options: When the output is larger than the source
Only when s = 1, that is when the output size equals the source size
When s is an integer, because the taps land on pixel centers
When nearest neighbour is used instead of bilinear
explain: The expression (s - 1) / 2 vanishes only at s = 1. Integer scale factors are the worst case for visibility, not the safe case: at s = 2 the shift is half a source pixel and at s = 4 it is 1.5 source pixels. Upscaling gives a negative shift, not zero.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
question: In a var-shape batch, the grid's x and y dimensions are sized from the largest image. What follows?
options: Blocks are launched for every image as if it were the largest, so a single outlier makes most blocks exit immediately at the bounds check
Smaller images are padded to the largest size before the kernel runs
The kernel must be launched once per distinct image size
Each image gets its own grid, so there is no waste
explain: z indexes the image and x and y tile the largest output, so every image's slice of the grid is as wide as the biggest one. For one 1920x1080 image among 31 small crops that is 65280 blocks launched against 3559 useful ones. No padding happens and the launch stays single: the waste is empty blocks, which is why batches are usually bucketed by size.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
question: In the fixed-segment toy, why could release_cached_blocks not rescue the Y2 allocation?
options: Because release_cached_blocks only works on the small pool
Because the device was out of virtual address space
Because Y2 was on a different stream
Because all cached free memory was inside segments that also held live tensors, and only whole unsplit segments can be released
explain: cudaFree releases a whole segment. Segments 1 to 3 each held a live 22 MiB tensor next to a 2 MiB hole, so none could be returned. The 22 MiB of unreserved memory alone was too small.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
question: Why did the V100 offsetCopy measurement lose only about 10% instead of the 20% the sector count predicts?
options: The V100 hardware realigns misaligned addresses for free
cudaMalloc pads arrays so that offsets never cross a sector
Adjacent warps reuse the over-fetched boundary sectors from cache
The kernel was limited by arithmetic, not memory
explain: Each warp's fifth sector is the next warp's first. The Best Practices Guide attributes the 9/10 result to adjacent warps reusing cache lines their neighbors fetched.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
question: On an H100, a kernel uses 256-thread blocks, 40 registers per thread and 32 KB of shared memory per block. Which resource limits occupancy?
options: Shared memory: 228/32 allows 7 blocks
Registers: 10,240 registers per block allows 6 blocks, fewer than the 7 that shared memory and the 8 that thread slots allow
Block slots: 32 resident blocks per SM
Nothing: the configuration reaches 100 percent occupancy
explain: Thread slots allow 2048/256 = 8 blocks; shared memory allows 228/32 = 7; registers need 40 x 32 = 1280 per warp and 8 x 1280 = 10,240 per block, so 65,536/10,240 = 6. The minimum is 6 blocks, 48 warps, 75 percent, and the limiter is the register file. Nsight Compute would show the same split across launch__occupancy_limit_registers, _shared_mem and _warps.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Computing a thread's global index: vector add end to end
question: A kernel uses `int i = threadIdx.x + blockDim.x * blockIdx.x;` and is launched with 4,000 blocks of 256 threads on an array of 1,000,000 floats, with no bounds check. What happens?
options: Fine: 4,000 x 256 is close enough to one million
Threads with i from 1,000,000 to 1,023,999 access memory past the end of the arrays
Only the first 3,907 blocks run; the runtime drops the rest automatically
The compiler inserts the bounds check because N is known
explain: 4,000 x 256 = 1,024,000 threads, so 24,000 threads have an index at or beyond N. Only 3907 blocks were needed (ceil of 1,000,000 / 256), and even then the last block would have 192 idle threads that need the `if (i < N)` check. Nothing drops blocks or adds checks for you.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
question: A Metal kernel assumes a SIMD-group is 32 wide and uses `thread_index_in_threadgroup / 32` to pick a SIMD-group's slot in threadgroup memory. What is the portable fix?
options: Nothing: every Metal GPU uses 32-wide SIMD-groups by specification
Use [[thread_position_in_grid]] / 32
Add threadgroup_barrier before the division
Use [[simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup]] (or divide by threads_per_simdgroup) instead of the constant 32
explain: MSL defines the SIMD-group width as a property you query (threads_per_simdgroup, or threadExecutionWidth on the host) and says the threadgroup is divided into SIMD-groups in an implementation-defined way. The built-in simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup gives the right answer on any GPU.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
question: You need to answer 200 broad questions a day over the same corpus and cost matters most. Based on the paper's Podcast results, which level is the best starting point?
options: C3, because it is most detailed
TS, because it reads the source text
C0, because it uses about 2.6% of TS's tokens while still beating vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity
Vector RAG, because it is cheapest
explain: The paper recommends root-level summaries for repeated global queries: dramatically fewer tokens with a modest drop versus other global methods. Vector RAG is cheapest but loses on comprehensiveness and diversity for these questions.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
question: A colleague says: "GRPO is cheaper because it does not need a reward model." What is the best correction?
options: Correct: GRPO never uses a reward model
GRPO removes the value model (critic); the reward can still come from a learned reward model or from a verifier
GRPO removes the reference model; the critic is still required
GRPO removes the policy's optimizer state by freezing most layers
explain: The saving comes from dropping the critic, a second trained network. DeepSeekMath's GRPO used a learned reward model. Whether the reward is a model or code is the separate RLVR question.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
question: R1-Zero's response length grew to thousands of tokens without any length reward. Which explanation fits the mechanism of GRPO with an outcome reward?
options: The KL penalty rewards longer outputs
The format reward pays per token
Outputs that reasoned longer were more often correct, so they got positive advantages and the habits that produced them were reinforced
The verifier counts reasoning steps
